laissez-faire

/les-ay-FAIR/ - rhymes with air · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Laissez-faire means favoring a hands-off approach, especially minimal government interference in markets.

The dorm's laissez-faire quiet-hours policy lasted exactly one midterm week.

Example

In the boomtown's first decade there was no building code at all. Lot owners raised whatever they liked — timber hotels six stories tall, chimneys leaning like question marks — and the council's official position was that a man's wall was his own business. The town wore its laissez-faire charter proudly right up until the fire of 1871 took eleven blocks in a night.

Laissez-faire is the exact word for that charter, because laissez-faire means favoring a hands-off approach, especially minimal government interference — not lazy oversight but a settled doctrine that the authorities should not meddle. A lenient inspector still inspects, gently; a laissez-faire council never sends one.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

permissive: Permissive is about what is allowed — a permissive curfew lets much happen. Laissez-faire is about what is managed: the authority could set terms and declines, on principle, to set them. A permissive board still grants the permissions; a laissez-faire board refuses to be the gatekeeper at all.

unregulated: Unregulated describes the field itself — a market or space where no rules apply at all. Laissez-faire describes the authority's stance toward the field: rules could be written, and the doctrine says leave it alone. An unregulated pond has no lifeguard chair; a laissez-faire pond keeps the chair empty on principle.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

interventionist: the state steps in on principle

controlling: a hand on every decision, large or small

Where it sits · how completely meddling is renounced — relaxed → hands-off → laissez-faire

relaxed vs. laissez-faire: Relaxed is the far shore from laissez-faire — the rules exist and are enforced, just gently, with the reins still firmly in hand.

hands-off vs. laissez-faire: Hands-off stops short of laissez-faire — a hands-off manager still watches and can step in; laissez-faire makes not interfering the official doctrine.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — laissez

Root — laissez: let, allow (French, from Latin laxare, to loosen)

Root — faire

Root — faire: to do, to make (French, from Latin facere)

Put it together

Put it together: Laissez (let) + faire (do) = let them do. The phrase is a whole French sentence fossilized into an English adjective — legend traces it to a merchant telling the French finance minister exactly what the government could do to help business: laissez-nous faire, let us do it ourselves.

Word Choice

formal / economic

Laissez-faire is doctrine vocabulary: it describes governments, policies, and management styles that refuse to intervene as a matter of principle. Hands-off is the plain twin; permissive is about what is allowed rather than what is managed. Among this unit's economics words it marks one pole — mercantilism has the state steering trade, corporatism seats industries inside the state, and laissez-faire sends the state home.
